text:
NORA. Only to sew on my costume. Good heavens, how unreasonable you are. (sits down on the sofa.) Now be nice, Doctor Rank; tomorrow you shall see how beautifully I shall dance; and then you must imagine that I am doing it only for your sake—yes, and then, of course, for Torvald’s; that goes without saying. (takes various things out of the box.) Doctor Rank, sit here, and I shall show you something.

RANK (sits down). What is it?

NORA. Look here. Look!

RANK. Silk stockings.

NORA. Flesh-colored. Aren’t they lovely? Yes, it is so dark in here now; but tomorrow—. No, no, no; you may only see the foot. Oh yes, you may indeed see the upper part too, if you like.

RANK. Hm—

NORA. Why do you look so critical? Perhaps you don’t think they will fit?

RANK. I cannot possibly have any well-founded opinion about that.

NORA (looks at him for a moment). Shame on you. (strikes him lightly on the ear with the stockings.) There, you deserve that. (packs them up again.)

RANK. And what other delights am I to be allowed to see?

NORA. You shall not see another scrap, because you are naughty.

(she hums a little and searches among the things.)

RANK (after a short silence). When I sit here like this, quite intimately together with you, I cannot comprehend—no, I cannot grasp—what would have become of me if I had never come into this house.

NORA (smiles). Oh, I think that, deep down, you enjoy yourself quite well with us.

RANK (more softly, staring ahead). And then to have to leave it all—

NORA. Nonsense; you are not leaving it.

RANK (as before). —and not even be able to leave behind one poor token of gratitude; scarcely even a fleeting sense of loss—nothing but an empty place that can be filled by the first person who comes along.

NORA. And if I were now to ask you to—? No—

RANK. To what?

NORA. To give me a great proof of your friendship—

RANK. Yes, yes?

NORA. No, I mean—to do me an immensely great service—

RANK. Would you really, for once, make me so happy?

NORA. Oh, you do not even know what it is.

RANK. Very well, then; say it.

NORA. No, but I cannot, Doctor Rank; it is something so unreasonably great—advice and help and a service as well—

RANK. So much the better. I cannot imagine what you can mean. But do speak. Do I not have your confidence?

NORA. Yes, you do, as no one else does. You are my most faithful and best friend; you know that. That is why I shall tell you. Very well, then, Doctor Rank; there is something you must help me prevent. You know how deeply, how indescribably dearly Torvald loves me; he would never hesitate for a moment to give his life for my sake.

RANK (leaning toward her). Nora—do you think that he is the only one—?

NORA (with a slight start). Who—?

RANK. Who would gladly give his life for your sake.

NORA (heavily). I see.

RANK. I have sworn to myself that you should know it before I went away. I would never find a better opportunity.—Yes, Nora, now you know it. And now you also know that you can confide in me as in no one else.

NORA (rises; evenly and calmly). Let me pass.

RANK (makes way for her, but remains seated). Nora—

NORA (in the doorway to the hall). Helene, bring in the lamp.—(goes over toward the stove.) Oh, dear Doctor Rank, that was really horrid of you.

RANK (rises). That I have loved you just as deeply as anyone else has? Was that horrid?

NORA. No, but that you should go and tell me so. There was no need at all—

RANK. What do you mean? Did you know—?

(The maid enters with the lamp, puts it on the table, and goes out again.)

RANK. Nora—Mrs. Helmer—I ask you, did you know anything?

NORA. Oh, how do I know what I knew or did not know? I truly cannot tell you—. How could you be so clumsy, Doctor Rank! Everything was so good as it was.

RANK. Well, at any rate, you now know for certain that I am at your disposal, body and soul. And will you now speak openly?

NORA (looks at him). After this?

RANK. I beg you, let me know what it is.

NORA. You cannot know anything now.

RANK. Yes, yes. You must not punish me like this. Allow me to do for you whatever lies within human power.

NORA. Now you can do nothing for me.—Besides, I am sure I do not need any help. You will see that it is all merely imagination. Yes, certainly it is. Of course! (sits down in the rocking chair, looks at him, smiles.) You really are a fine gentleman, Doctor Rank. Don’t you think you ought to be ashamed of yourself now that the lamp has been brought in?

RANK. No; not really. But perhaps I should go—for good?

NORA. No, you certainly must not do that. Of course you must come here as before. You know very well that Torvald cannot do without you.

RANK. Yes, but you?

NORA. Oh, I always think it becomes tremendously enjoyable here when you come.

RANK. That is precisely what led me astray. You are a riddle to me. Many times it has seemed to me that you would almost as gladly be with me as with Helmer.

NORA. Yes, you see, there are some people whom one loves most, and other people whom one would almost rather be with.

RANK. Oh yes, there is something in that.

NORA. When I was at home, naturally I loved Papa most. But I always thought it was so immensely amusing when I could steal downstairs to the maids’ room; for they did not guide me in the least, and they always talked about so many amusing things among themselves.

RANK. Aha; so it is they whom I have replaced.

NORA (springs up and goes over to him). Oh, dear, kind Doctor Rank, I did not mean that at all. But surely you can understand that with Torvald it is just as it was with Papa—

(The maid comes in from the hall.)

MAID. Madam! (whispers and hands her a card.)

NORA (glances at the card). Ah! (puts it in her pocket.)

RANK. Is something wrong?

NORA. No, no, not at all; it is only something—it is my new costume—

RANK. What? Your costume is lying right there.

NORA. Oh yes, that one; but this is another; I have ordered it—Torvald must not know—

RANK. Aha, so there we have the great secret.

NORA. Yes, indeed; just go in to him; he is sitting in the inner room; keep him occupied for a while—

RANK. Do not worry; he shall not get away from me. (he goes into Helmer’s room.)

NORA (to the maid). And he is standing waiting in the kitchen?

MAID. Yes, he came up the back stairs—

NORA. But didn’t you tell him that someone was here?

MAID. Yes, but it did no good.

NORA. He will not go away again?

MAID. No, he will not go until he has spoken with Madam.
